title: LatticePay - Streaming SLA & Latency Benchmark Probe
summary: Intro discovery to map p95 latency targets, streaming behavior, concurrency, and token/sec benchmarking needs for an embedded payments fraud chat assistant. Customer evaluating Hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC) deployment; wants pilot benchmark and security docs.
topics: expected concurrency and steady-state vs burst behavior
hosted vs Dedicated vs Private (VPC/on-prem) tradeoffs
security: SOC2, SSO, KMS, audit logs
benchmark plan and next steps for pilot
transcript:
[00:00] Samir: Hi everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samir from Redwood Inference, and with me is Leah and Tom on the engineering side. How's everyone doing?
[00:08] Maya: Good, thanks. Excited to dig in — we've been talking about latency issues with our payments chat assistant.
[00:15] Rahul: Hey, quick context — we serve low-latency decisioning in the payments flow, so p95 is basically our S L A from a product perspective. We get spikes at midnight, end of month, and during promos.
[00:28] Leah: Got it. Out of curiosity, what's the current architecture? Are you calling an external LLM now or self-hosting?
[00:34] Elena: We have an internal microservice that hits an external provider now, yes. It's fairly synchronous — we stream partial answers back to the UI but often fall back to non-streaming when network jitter hits.
[00:46] Samir: Cool. High-level, we'll map your p95 targets and then propose a benchmark plan. Typical questions: target p95 for streaming responses, expected concurrent sessions, average and max token lengths.
[00:56] Maya: For the payments assistant, target p95 is 300ms for short prompts (about 30-80 tokens), and 800ms for longer flows (~300 tokens). That's our internal target — we know it's tight.
[01:10] Rahul: Concurrently we expect 150 steady concurrency and bursts to 1,200 for 3-5 minutes. Token/sec at bursts is roughly 20k-30k tokens/sec across the fleet.
[01:22] Tom: That burst profile is helpful. For clarity: are those streaming token rates or total aggregate tokens consumed?
[01:27] Rahul: Aggregate streamed tokens — a lot of partials, so streaming efficiency matters.
[01:31] Leah: Great. On Redwood side, we have three serving modes — Hosted API, Dedicated reserved capacity, and Private (VPC / customer-managed). Each has different routing and fallback options, and there are tradeoffs around control and latency.
[01:44] Elena: Can you give a concrete example of how latency differs between Hosted vs Dedicated for p95 streaming?
[01:50] Leah: Sure. Roughly, for a 30-token streaming write on our Hosted tier, customers often see p95 in the 200-400ms range depending on region and network; Dedicated we tune the GPU pool and batching for lower tail latency and typically see better p95 under high concurrency because capacity is reserved — so p95 can drop to 150-250ms. Private is similar to Dedicated if you colocate near your app, but networking and infra variability matters.
[02:12] Maya: Are those numbers validated with token/sec benchmarks or just observed?
[02:16] Leah: Observed in benchmarks and customer configs — we always recommend running a microbenchmark with your real prompts because sequence length distribution and model choice change the numbers.
[02:25] Samir: Also important: KV cache/prefix caching can shave a lot of costs and latency on repeated prompts — though the caching hit rate depends on your prompt patterns.
[02:34] Rahul: We have a lot of shared boilerplate in prompts, so caching should help. Quick Q on quantization: does Redwood support quantized variants for Dedicated?
[02:44] Tom: Yes, our runtime supports multiple quantization profiles and will route to compatible kernels. We do automatic kernel selection and quantization-aware execution paths, but for Private deployments customers often choose which quantization levels they accept for accuracy tradeoffs.
[02:57] Maya: Security — we need SOC2, SSO integration (SAML), VPC peering or private link, and KMS integration for keys. Is audit logging available per-token or per-request?
[03:09] Leah: We store request metadata and have audit logs in Dedicated and Private; Hosted can be configured to meet stricter retention with an enterprise add-on. KMS/HSM integrations are supported in Private, and we have SAML SSO + RBAC. We'll share the security pack.
[03:22] Elena: Great. On fallback behaviors — if we lose Dedicated capacity during a huge burst, do you have automated fallback to Hosted or a smaller model variant to preserve availability?
[03:32] Samir: Yes, routing policies can failover to compatible model variants or to Hosted. You can configure canary and A/B rollouts and automatic fallback policies in the Console. Fallback latency will depend on the target model/region.
[03:44] Rahul: For the benchmark we'll need to see p95 at 150 steady concurrency and at 1,200 burst — ideally both streaming p95 and token/sec throughput.
[03:53] Leah: That aligns with our standard surge tests. Proposed plan: run an initial microbenchmark in Hosted to get a baseline with your prompts, then run Dedicated sandbox with similar hardware to measure steady-state and burst. For Private we can advise on network topology impacts.
[04:05] Maya: Timeline? We want results before committing to a vendor by mid-May.
[04:10] Samir: We can kick a pilot the week of May 4, initial baseline in Hosted in 3 business days, Dedicated sandbox tests by week of May 11.
[04:18] Elena: Who owns the benchmark harness — Redwood or LatticePay?
[04:21] Leah: We'll provide a harness template (k6 + token streaming harness + sample scripts) and run the first pass ourselves with your prompts, then hand over the harness.
[04:30] Damien: A note on compliance — we have to vet network egress and data retention. Hosted may not be acceptable for some flows.
[04:36] Samir: Understood. For regulated flows you typically see customers pick Dedicated or Private to keep data siloed and control retention. We'll include retention configs and our data processing agreement.
[04:46] Rahul: Let's talk measurement specifics: when you report p95 for streaming, are you measuring time-to-first-token, time-to-95%-tokens, or end-to-end response?
[04:55] Tom: Good question. We report several latency metrics: TTF (time-to-first-token), TTR (time-to-response / final token), and streaming tail like p95 of each token event. For your UI you might care more about TTF and steady token emission rate.
[05:08] Maya: If we target 300ms p95 for short flows, is TTF the right metric?
[05:12] Leah: Usually yes. For short 30-80 token prompts TTF dominates perceived latency. For longer multi-stage flows the aggregated TTR and sustained tokens/sec matter.
[05:21] Elena: What about multiplexing or request batching on Dedicated — does that introduce extra tail latency?
[05:27] Tom: We do continuous batching with workload-aware policies. Batching reduces cost at some latency tradeoff; the runtime is optimized for tail latency with preemption and kernel selection, but extremely high concurrency may increase batching-induced tail. Configurable autoscaling and burst pools help maintain p95.
[05:40] Rahul: Autoscaling speeds? For bursts of 1,200 from 150, can we get capacity up fast enough?
[05:45] Leah: We have burst pools and configurable warm capacity; Dedicated customers often reserve burst GPU capacity or configure fast autoscaling windows. For critical flows, we recommend reserved burst nodes to meet p95 targets.
[05:56] Maya: Can you run an initial test with model X and Y? We want to compare a 7B and a 13B variant.
[06:03] Leah: Yes. Please share the exact model names — we can test both. We'll also run quantized variants for Dedicated.
[06:09] Elena: Any concerns about hallucinations when you quantize?
[06:14] Tom: There is a small accuracy delta depending on quantization. We'll include quality checks in the benchmark and compare outputs against baselines.
[06:21] Rahul: On instrumentation — we need per-route token and cost breakdowns, and tracing hooks to connect requests to our tracing system.
[06:29] Samir: Console supports token-level cost and latency breakdowns, and tracing hooks. For Private, you can send logs to your ELK/Datadog.
[06:37] Maya: Good. Are there regional constraints? We run mostly in us-east-1 and eu-west-1.
[06:41] Leah: We can run benchmarks in either region. For Hosted we have multi-region endpoints; Dedicated and Private are typically in the region you specify.
[06:49] Elena: Pricing — rough delta between Hosted and Dedicated for burst-heavy workloads?
[06:53] Samir: Hosted is usage-based, good for low commitment; Dedicated has a monthly reserved capacity with lower per-token cost and predictable throughput. For burst-heavy patterns, Dedicated with reserved burst nodes is often more economical. We'll provide a cost modeling spreadsheet in the follow-up.
[07:06] Rahul: On the microbenchmark, we need to define success criteria: 300ms p95 TTF for short flows, 800ms p95 TTR for long flows, <10% degradation during 5-minute bursts, and sustained tokens/sec above 20k during bursts.
[07:18] Leah: That seems realistic. We'll record TTF/TTR/p95 and tokens/sec under your concurrency profile and return a report with histograms and tail analysis.
[07:28] Maya: Can you simulate our network variance too? We have up to 70ms added jitter for some mobile clients.
[07:33] Tom: We'll include network shaping in the hosted test. For Private and Dedicated you'll get more control over egress latency.
[07:40] Elena: Any limits on streaming open connections? We could have thousands of open websockets for user sessions.
[07:46] Leah: We support streaming over websockets and HTTP/2, and connection scaling is managed by the edge. For extremely large numbers of persistent connections we recommend a connection fronting layer (load balancer / websocket gateway) and Redwood's streaming endpoints behind it.
[07:58] Rahul: For the benchmark harness, can you run both TTF-first-token and entire-token-latency metrics with percentiles at p50/p90/p95/p99?
[08:06] Leah: Yes, we'll produce those percentiles and a CSV/JSON of raw events.
[08:10] Maya: We'll provide three canonical prompt flows with expected token lengths and a smaller random sample set for guardrails.
[08:15] Samir: Perfect. Security doc drop — we'll attach SOC2/ISO summary, network diagrams, and the DPA.
[08:21] Damien: Please include details on key rotation for KMS, and whether logs can be pushed to our AWS account.
[08:26] Tom: For Private, keys stay in your KMS. For Hosted and Dedicated we provide KMS integrations; logs can be exported to your S3/Cloudwatch with proper IAM. We'll document specifics.
[08:37] Elena: Can you show an example of a fallback policy in the Console?
[08:41] Leah: We'll include screenshots in the follow-up deck and a sample routing policy: primary Dedicated model -> fallback to hosted lightweight variant -> degrade to cached answer.
[08:51] Maya: What about rate limits and quotas? We need sustained throughput at 20k tokens/sec but also burst headroom; how do quotas interact with burst pools?
[08:59] Samir: Quotas in Hosted are per-account with rate limiting. In Dedicated you control policies and can allocate burst capacity; quotas are mostly for governance. We'll show how to set route-level quotas in the Console.
[09:12] Rahul: Any internal examples of customers with similar numbers?
[09:15] Leah: We have a payments customer with similar burst patterns who moved to Dedicated plus reserved burst nodes; their p95 improved 35% during peaks.
[09:24] Elena: Fine. Let's recap and next steps.
[09:28] Samir: Recap: you shared targets (300ms p95 short, 800ms p95 long, 150 steady concurrency, 1,200 bursts, 20k-30k tokens/sec burst). Redwood will: 1) run Hosted baseline with your prompts, 2) spin Dedicated sandbox for steady and burst tests, 3) produce a report with TTF/TTR/p95/p99 and tokens/sec, and 4) provide security docs and pricing.
[09:44] Maya: Timeline?
[09:46] Samir: Kick pilot week of May 4, baseline results in ~3 business days, Dedicated tests by week of May 11, final report by May 18.
[09:54] Elena: Sounds good.
[09:56] Tom: Quick technical note — please share a sample tokenization or we can tokenize on our side to ensure token counts match.
[10:02] Maya: We'll send prompt set and a sample tokenization.
[10:05] Rahul: Also share your benchmark harness and the pricing spreadsheet.
[10:08] Samir: Will do. Thanks everyone, we'll follow up with calendar invites and the documents.
[10:14] Maya: Thanks.
[10:16] Elena: Thanks, bye.
